location: Pacific Ocean, approximately 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, California
the_unresolved_thing: Whether the mechanical stop (lower end play) fractured in-flight or upon impact, and the precise sequence of failure of the gimbal nut threads relative to torque tube fracture.

structural_test.why: The investigation did settle the primary mechanical cause (acme nut thread failure from insufficient lubrication), but early in the investigation a real disagreement existed over whether the mechanical stop broke in-flight (shifting liability toward Boeing design) versus on impact. The NTSB's final report attributes the uncontrollable dive to torque tube fracture followed by fairing bracket failure, but contemporaneous statements from Boeing and NTSB investigators reflect unresolved questions about exact sequence and timing.

commonly_wrong.claim: The mechanical stop (end play) broke off and that's what caused the uncontrollable dive.
commonly_wrong.record: The cause of the final dive was the low-cycle fatigue fracture of the torque tube, followed by failure of the vertical stabilizer tip fairing brackets, which allowed the horizontal stabilizer leading edge to move upward well beyond what a normally operating jackscrew assembly permits, creating excessive upward aerodynamic tail load and uncontrollable downward pitching.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: Collapses two distinct failure events into one, obscuring that the jackscrew's acme nut thread loss and the later structural fracture were separate stages of the accident sequence.

commonly_wrong.claim: The jackscrew itself broke during flight.
commonly_wrong.record: The acme nut threads on the jackscrew failed and stripped away. Later analysis estimated 90% of the threads in the acme nut had been previously worn away, and were completely sheared off during the accident flight.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The jackscrew (the shaft) survived; it was the acme nut riding on it that lost its threads. Confusing the two misattributes the failure mode.

commonly_wrong.claim: This was purely a random mechanical failure with no warning.
commonly_wrong.record: Two years earlier, a lead mechanic at Alaska Airlines' Oakland maintenance facility found the jackscrew end play worn to its maximum limit of 0.040 inch and ordered it replaced. The aircraft was returned to service days later with the worn assembly still installed.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: There was a documented maintenance flag on this exact assembly years before the crash, which matters for any claim that the failure was unforeseeable.

investigators_disagree.question: Did the mechanical stop (lower end play) fracture in-flight or on impact with the ocean?
investigators_disagree.position_a: NTSB investigator Dan Bowers determined that re-creating the final part of the dive required tilting the stabilizer up 22 degrees, achievable only if the jackscrew separated from the end stop before impact.
investigators_disagree.position_b: Boeing spokeswoman Liz Verdier stated: 'Everyone agrees that it did break off but we don't know where' or when — leaving open whether it failed in flight or on impact.
investigators_disagree.status: The NTSB's final report settled on torque tube fracture and fairing bracket failure as the mechanism for the final uncontrollable dive, but the precise timing of end-stop separation relative to other failures was not conclusively fixed in contemporaneous investigative statements.

could_not_verify.item: Whether Alaska Airlines specifically used an unapproved type of grease on the jackscrew assembly (one source claims MIL-G-23827 instead of MIL-G-81322)
could_not_verify.note: Not directly quoted from NTSB AAR-02/01; only found in secondary sources.

could_not_verify.item: Exact details of the tools used in the end-play check and whether they were non-standard
could_not_verify.note: Mentioned in secondary sources but not directly accessed from the official docket.

could_not_verify.item: Specific words spoken by the pilots on the CVR transcript

caption:
88 people died when Alaska Airlines Flight 261 went into the Pacific Ocean 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, California, on January 31, 2000.
The NTSB traced the crash to a worn acme nut on the horizontal stabilizer jackscrew — a part flagged for replacement two years earlier. What investigators never fully pinned down was exactly when the mechanical stop failed relative to the final structural fracture.
Source: NTSB/AAR-02/01; NTSB Docket DCA00MA023.

longform_note: Tier C only. The primary mechanical cause (acme nut thread wear from insufficient lubrication) is settled and well-documented — this is a correction/artifact post, not a mystery case. The one open thread (timing of end-stop fracture, in-flight vs. impact) is a footnote-level dispute among investigators, not a load-bearing unresolved question, and does not meet the bar for long-form.

location: Bank of America branch, North Hollywood, Los Angeles
agency: Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD); incident response
the_number: 44 minutes duration; 2,000+ rounds exchanged; 11 officers and 7 bystanders wounded; 0 civilian/officer fatalities
the_unresolved_thing: LAPD patrol shotguns were restricted to buckshot-only ammunition at the time of the incident. No primary source—including the official LAPD Use of Force Review Board report filed June 12, 1998—documents who authorized this ammunition restriction, on what ballistic or policy grounds, or whether any safety recommendation about patrol armament standards was formally issued, accepted, or closed as unacceptable. The regulation permitting the condition that failed was never revisited or challenged in surviving official records.

structural_test.why: PASS—regulatory approval chain unresolved. The mechanism (buckshot cannot defeat rifle-rated body armor) is well understood; who set that ammunition policy and why is not.

commonly_wrong.claim: Officers were armed with rifles from the beginning of the encounter
commonly_wrong.record: Patrol officers initially carried only sidearms. Per the after-action report, officers did not confirm the suspects wore body armor until 9:33 a.m., roughly 16 minutes into the incident, then improvised by obtaining AR-15s from a nearby civilian gun dealer, B&B Gun Sales.
commonly_wrong.source: LAPD Use of Force Review Board Report, June 12, 1998
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The 16-minute gap is the entire structural failure the department later had to account for.

commonly_wrong.claim: The suspects used true armor-piercing ammunition
commonly_wrong.record: Media reported 'armor-piercing bullets,' but the robbers used standard high-velocity rifle ammunition—7.62×39mm and 5.56mm—not formally designated AP rounds. No independent ballistic test of the actual rounds used appears in the surviving docket.
commonly_wrong.source: Secondary reporting cross-checked against available docket materials; no ballistic test report located
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The gap between handgun and rifle rounds, not exotic ammunition, is what defeated patrol officers' weapons.

commonly_wrong.claim: SWAT rifles were immediately effective once they arrived
commonly_wrong.record: SWAT arrived 18 minutes after first shots. AR-15 fire had little effect on the heaviest armored areas; fatal hits came from unarmored zones—Phillips' hand and a self-inflicted head wound, Matasareanu's legs after a SWAT officer fired beneath a vehicle undercarriage.
commonly_wrong.source: Wikipedia summary cross-referenced with after-action narrative; primary ballistic detail not fully documented in surviving docket
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The ending is often flattened into 'SWAT rifles won'; the record shows armor gaps, not rifle superiority, ended it.

investigators_disagree.question: How many officers and bystanders were wounded?
investigators_disagree.position_a: NBC Los Angeles and Wikipedia: 11 officers, 7 bystanders wounded
investigators_disagree.status: Police1.com reports 11 officers, 6 bystanders; other outlets cite 12 and 8. The 1998 LAPD report should be the controlling figure, but public secondary sources have never converged.

could_not_verify.note: No layer count, Kevlar weight, or construction detail located in primary sources.

could_not_verify.note: Central to the unresolved thread; stated as unresolved, not asserted either way.

could_not_verify.note: No such document located; absence itself is part of the unresolved claim.

caption:
44 minutes. 2,000+ rounds fired. 11 officers and 7 bystanders wounded. Zero deaths among them.
Two robbers in homemade body armor fought LAPD patrol officers armed with handguns and buckshot-loaded shotguns—neither could penetrate. The 1998 Use of Force Review Board report never establishes who restricted patrol shotguns to buckshot in the first place, or whether that restriction was ever formally reviewed.
Source: LAPD Board of Police Commissioners, Use of Force Review Board Report, June 12, 1998.
34.1899° N, 118.3764° W
x_post: Everyone says LAPD officers were simply outgunned on Feb 28, 1997. The 1998 Use of Force Review Board report says something narrower: patrol shotguns were restricted to buckshot only. No surviving record says who set that restriction, or why it was never revisited.

hook_alternates.hook: Page one of the 1998 LAPD Use of Force Review Board report doesn't name who restricted patrol shotguns to buckshot.
Minute 16: officers confirm the robbers' armor stops their bullets. Minute 18: SWAT arrives with rifles.
LAPD had 600 military rifles within the year. On Feb 28, 1997, officers borrowed guns from a gun store.

longform_note: Long-form candidate: full docket exists (LAPD Use of Force Review Board Report, June 12, 1998), and the unresolved thread is institutional, not forensic—the ammunition-restriction approval chain, not the mechanics of the firefight. Structure the episode around the 44-minute timeline, then pivot at minute 30 to the open question: no surviving record shows who authorized buckshot-only patrol shotguns, whether any post-incident safety recommendation on patrol armament was issued, or whether it was ever closed. Avoid treating Phillips or Matasareanu's tactics as the causal center; the systemic gap is the armament policy, not the robbers' preparation.
